title: Transformers and the National Grid
description: Use the transformer equation Vp/Vs = Np/Ns and power balance to solve National Grid problems step-up and step-down.
hero_keywords: electricity pylon high voltage power line
hero_image_caption: Hundreds of thousands of volts surge through the National Grid — transformers make this possible, stepping voltages up and down with almost no energy loss.
content_html:
Electromagnetic Induction and How Transformers Work

A transformer works by electromagnetic induction. When an alternating current (a.c.) flows through the primary coil, it creates an alternating magnetic field in the iron core. This changing field passes through the secondary coil, inducing an alternating potential difference (voltage) across it. This only works with a.c. — a steady direct current (d.c.) would produce a constant magnetic field that induces no voltage.

The ratio of the voltages across the two coils depends on the ratio of the number of turns (loops of wire) in each coil. The more turns in the secondary coil relative to the primary, the higher the output voltage. The fewer turns, the lower the output voltage.

Key Fact

Transformer turns ratio equation (given on your exam equation sheet): $$\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}$$ where \(V_p\) = primary voltage (V), \(V_s\) = secondary voltage (V), \(N_p\) = number of turns in primary coil, \(N_s\) = number of turns in secondary coil. A common error is inverting the ratio — keep primary on top on both sides.

Step-Up and Step-Down Transformers

A step-up transformer has more turns in the secondary than the primary (\(N_s > N_p\)), so the output voltage is greater than the input voltage. A step-down transformer has fewer secondary turns (\(N_s < N_p\)), reducing the voltage. Transformers can only increase or decrease voltage — they cannot create energy. If voltage goes up, current goes down proportionally, and vice versa.

Question: A transformer has 500 turns on the primary coil and 5000 turns on the secondary coil. The primary voltage is 230 V. Calculate the secondary voltage.

Step 1: Identify values. \(V_p\) = 230 V, \(N_p\) = 500, \(N_s\) = 5000.

Step 2: Rearrange \(\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}\) for \(V_s\): $$V_s = V_p \times \frac{N_s}{N_p} = 230 \times \frac{5000}{500} = 230 \times 10 = 2300 \text{ V}$$

Step 3: State: The secondary voltage is 2300 V. This is a step-up transformer (\(N_s > N_p\), \(V_s > V_p\)).

Tip: Notice that \(N_s/N_p = 10\), so \(V_s = 10 \times V_p\). The turns ratio directly multiplies the voltage.

The Power Equation for Transformers

An ideal transformer transfers all power from the primary to the secondary — no energy is lost. Since power \(P = V \times I\), and power is conserved: $$V_p \times I_p = V_s \times I_s$$ This is given on your exam equation sheet. If the voltage increases, the current must decrease by the same factor to keep power constant. This explains why a step-up transformer produces a higher voltage but a lower current.

Question: A step-up transformer has a primary voltage of 25 000 V and a primary current of 200 A. The secondary voltage is 400 000 V. Calculate the secondary current, assuming an ideal transformer.

Step 1: Identify values. \(V_p\) = 25 000 V, \(I_p\) = 200 A, \(V_s\) = 400 000 V.

Step 2: Rearrange \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\) for \(I_s\): $$I_s = \frac{V_p \times I_p}{V_s} = \frac{25\,000 \times 200}{400\,000} = \frac{5\,000\,000}{400\,000} = 12.5 \text{ A}$$

Step 3: The secondary current is 12.5 A. As voltage increased by a factor of 16, current decreased by a factor of 16 (from 200 A to 12.5 A). Power is conserved: \(25\,000 \times 200 = 400\,000 \times 12.5 = 5\,000\,000\) W ✓.

The National Grid

The National Grid transmits electrical power across the country from power stations to consumers. The key challenge is minimising energy losses in the cables, which occur as heat whenever a current flows through the resistance of the wire. The power dissipated as heat is given by \(P = I^2 R\). Because power lost depends on the square of the current, reducing the current dramatically reduces losses.

Step-up transformers at the power station increase the voltage to very high values (hundreds of thousands of volts). By the power equation \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\), this high voltage corresponds to a very small current in the transmission cables. The power loss (\(I^2 R\)) is therefore tiny. Near homes and businesses, step-down transformers reduce the voltage to the safe level used for domestic supply — in the UK, this is approximately 230 V a.c. at a frequency of 50 Hz.

Key Fact

High-voltage transmission reduces current. Because power lost as heat = I²R, a small current means very little energy is wasted as heat in the cables. Step-up transformers raise the voltage (and reduce current) for transmission; step-down transformers lower it to a safe level for domestic use.

Alternating Current and the Domestic Supply

Alternating current (a.c.) continuously changes direction. In the UK, the domestic mains supply is a.c. at a frequency of 50 Hz (50 complete cycles per second) and an rms voltage of approximately 230 V. Transformers require a.c. because only a changing current produces a changing magnetic field, which is essential for electromagnetic induction. Direct current (d.c.) from a battery produces a steady field and will not induce a voltage in the secondary coil of a transformer.
exam_tip_html: The most common exam error with the transformer equation is inverting the turns ratio. Remember: primary over secondary equals primary over secondary — \(V_p / V_s = N_p / N_s\). Keep the same fraction on both sides. For National Grid questions, you must explain why high voltage is used by linking it to the \(P = I^2 R\) equation — saying 'to reduce energy loss' alone is not enough. You need to state that high voltage means low current, and low current means much less power lost as heat (since \(P \propto I^2\)). Also note that the spec requires you to know that UK domestic supply is a.c. at 50 Hz and approximately 230 V.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Transformer turns ratio: \(V_p / V_s = N_p / N_s\). Step-up: more secondary turns → higher output voltage. Step-down: fewer secondary turns → lower output voltage.
  • Power is conserved in an ideal transformer: \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\). Higher voltage means proportionally lower current.
  • The National Grid uses step-up transformers to transmit at high voltage and low current, minimising power loss (\(I^2 R\)) in cables. Step-down transformers near homes reduce voltage to the safe domestic level (approximately 230 V a.c. at 50 Hz in the UK).

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following statements about transformers is correct?
A) Transformers work with both alternating and direct current
B) A step-up transformer increases voltage and current simultaneously
C) The secondary voltage depends on the ratio of turns in the two coils
D) Transformers create electrical energy from mechanical energy
practice_questions.marks: C) The secondary voltage depends on the ratio of turns in the two coils [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the equation that links the voltages and number of turns in a transformer.
practice_questions.marks: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns [1 mark — accept equivalent forms]

practice_questions.text: Describe why the National Grid transmits electrical power at a high voltage rather than a low voltage.
practice_questions.marks: High voltage means a lower current in the cables (1). Lower current means less power is lost as heat in the cables / power loss = I²R so lower I means less loss (1). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a transformer works. In your answer, include the role of alternating current and the iron core.
practice_questions.marks: An alternating current in the primary coil creates an alternating/changing magnetic field (1). The iron core carries/concentrates this changing magnetic field to the secondary coil (1). The changing magnetic field in the secondary coil induces an alternating potential difference / voltage across it (1). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A transformer at a power station has 200 turns on the primary coil and 40 000 turns on the secondary coil. The primary voltage is 25 000 V and the primary current is 500 A.
(a) Calculate the secondary voltage.
(b) Calculate the secondary current, assuming an ideal transformer.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Vp / Vs = Np / Ns → Vs = Vp × (Ns / Np) = 25 000 × (40 000 / 200) = 25 000 × 200 = 5 000 000 V (or 5 MV) [2 marks: 1 for method, 1 for correct answer with unit]
(b) Vp × Ip = Vs × Is → Is = (Vp × Ip) / Vs = (25 000 × 500) / 5 000 000 = 12 500 000 / 5 000 000 = 2.5 A [2 marks: 1 for method, 1 for correct answer with unit] [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that 'transformers are perfectly efficient devices.' In your answer, discuss the principle of energy conservation in an ideal transformer, the equation Vp × Ip = Vs × Is, and the reasons why real transformers lose a small amount of energy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): States that in an ideal transformer, energy is conserved — all power input equals power output, giving Vp × Ip = Vs × Is. Explains that if voltage is stepped up, current is stepped down proportionally so power remains constant. Acknowledges that real transformers are not perfectly efficient — energy is lost as heat in the resistance of the coils, and as 'eddy currents' induced in the iron core (candidates do not need to use the term 'eddy currents' but should reference heat losses in the core or coil). Concludes that while very close to ideal (modern large transformers are typically over 99% efficient), real transformers do lose some energy. Awarded top band only if the candidate uses correct physics throughout and reaches a justified conclusion about the extent to which the claim is valid.
Secure (3–4 marks): Correctly states energy conservation in ideal transformer and the power equation. Notes that real transformers have some losses but may not explain the mechanism fully.
Developing (1–2 marks): Recognises that power in equals power out for ideal case, or mentions real losses, but treatment is incomplete. [6 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: A transformer has 100 turns on the primary and 2000 turns on the secondary. The primary voltage is 12 V. What is the secondary voltage?
Why must the current in the National Grid transmission cables be as small as possible?
options: Smaller current means higher voltage is not needed
Power lost as heat = I²R, so a smaller current dramatically reduces energy losses
Smaller current prevents the cables from expanding in warm weather
The transformers only work with small currents

knowledge_checks.q: A step-up transformer increases voltage from 1000 V to 20 000 V. If the primary current is 400 A, what is the secondary current in an ideal transformer: _____
Why do transformers only work with alternating current: _____
options: Direct current would overheat the iron core
Only a changing current produces a changing magnetic field, which is needed to induce a voltage in the secondary coil
Alternating current is at the correct voltage for the turns ratio to work
Direct current cannot pass through an iron core
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is Only a changing current produces a changing magnetic field, which is needed to induce a voltage in the secondary coil.

knowledge_checks.explanation: Review the key terms and definitions covered in this lesson.

flashcard_questions.q: State the transformer turns ratio equation.
flashcard_questions.a: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns, where Vp and Vs are primary and secondary voltages, and Np and Ns are the number of turns.

flashcard_questions.q: State the power equation for an ideal transformer.
flashcard_questions.a: Vp × Ip = Vs × Is. Power in equals power out; if voltage increases, current decreases proportionally.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a step-up transformer and where is it used in the National Grid?
flashcard_questions.a: A transformer where the secondary has more turns than the primary, increasing voltage. Step-up transformers are used at power stations to raise voltage for long-distance transmission.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the National Grid transmit power at high voltage?
flashcard_questions.a: High voltage means low current. Since power lost = I²R, a lower current greatly reduces energy wasted as heat in the transmission cables.

flashcard_questions.q: What principle of electromagnetic induction makes a transformer work?
flashcard_questions.a: An alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing magnetic field in the iron core. This changing field induces an alternating voltage in the secondary coil.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the approximate domestic mains supply in the UK?
flashcard_questions.a: Approximately 230 V alternating current at 50 Hz.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does a transformer not work with direct current?
flashcard_questions.a: Direct current produces a constant magnetic field. Only a changing magnetic field can induce a voltage in the secondary coil, which requires alternating current.

glossary_terms.definition: A device that uses electromagnetic induction to change the voltage of an alternating current supply.
The process by which a changing magnetic field in a conductor induces a potential difference across it.
The input coil of a transformer, connected to the supply voltage.
The output coil of a transformer, from which the transformed voltage is taken.
A transformer in which the secondary coil has more turns than the primary, increasing the output voltage.
A transformer in which the secondary coil has fewer turns than the primary, decreasing the output voltage.
The network of cables and transformers that distributes electricity generated at power stations to homes and businesses across the country.
An electric current that reverses direction repeatedly at a fixed frequency.
